For the officer joining this caseload, here is a concise orientation note:  

**District Concentration**: Cases are concentrated in **فیصل آباد (Faisalabad)** (19 cases), **لاہور (Lahore)** (18 cases), and **راولپنڈی (Rawalpindi)** (10 cases), with smaller numbers in other districts [Document 1].  

**Case Mix**: The caseload now includes **39 FIRs** under the **Pakistan Penal Code (PPC)**, **12 under CNSA 1997**, **9 under PECA 2016**, and others involving domestic violence, illegal dispossession, and cybercrimes — a marked shift from 2024, which focused on arms-related offenses and robbery/conspiracy [Document 2].  

**Arrests**: Only **11 of 73 FIRs** record at least one arrest, while **62 FIRs** have no arrests (e.g., accused under investigation or absconding) [Document 3].  

**Reporting Delays**: The mean time from incident to report is **≈23.4 hours** (1401.3 minutes) in 2026, compared to **15 minutes** in 2024 — indicating significantly slower reporting now [Document 4].  

**Weapon Licensing**: **30 cases** involve recovered weapons with **no licence recorded**, and **2 cases** have no licence status noted at all [Document 5].  

**Accused Profile**: Of **92 accused**, only **17 have recorded ages** (24–49 years, mean 31.5), while **75 have no age data**. Relationships with complainants are recorded in **10 FIRs**, with **‘اجنبی (stranger)’** being the most common (15 of 24 entries) [Document 6][Document 7].  

**Court Progress**: Of **33 criminal records**, **32 are still in progress**, and only **1 case** has reached a verdict (conviction with bail pending appeal) [Document 8].  

This caseload requires attention to delayed reporting, diverse legal frameworks, and low arrest rates, with a focus on weapon licensing and cross-checking accused relationships.
